newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU grain award pleases some, tantalises others.
newsitem.headline: EU grain award pleases some, tantalises others.

text.p: The European Union offered a concession to angry grain exporters by increasing wheat sales on Thursday but coupled this with a tough signal that it would scrutinise every penny of subsidy in the coming weeks, traders said.

The European Commission, assailed by traders who wanted subsidies to export up to a million tonnes to meet partly loss-making contracts, granted subsidies up to 12.90 Ecus per tonne to cover shipments of 398,500 tonnes of wheat.
At a previous weekly tender it had released 238,000 tonnes with subsidies of up to 16.40 Ecus per tonne.

The refund, designed to bridge the gap with lower world prices, fell after traders sharply lowered their bids for subsidies in order to catch up with an unfulfilled order book estimated by some analysts at more than 1.2 million tonnes.
The new volume was also within striking distance of the EU's weekly export record for the current grain year (July/June) of 450,000 tonnes, traders said.
But while several welcomed this, others were infuriated that for just a fraction of an Ecu more in subsidy, Brussels could have allowed them to export another 100,000 tonnes.
Traders bid for subsidies at a weekly tender, hoping their idea of the refund rate needed to match world markets is as close as possible to the maximum rebate actually awarded.
While the Commission set the cut-off at 12.90 Ecus per tonne, unpublished bidding details showed another 120,000 tonnes of wheat had been sandwiched between 12.90 and 13 Ecus.
Traders with contracts to sell these volumes therefore had their bids rejected and sources said they would be furious.
"It is ridiculous. For a tenth of an Ecu more they could have exported half a million tonnes instead of moving the goalposts on us again," said one export source.
Analysts said the decision, endorsed by member states at weekly grain talks, showed the Commission was ready to bow to some requests and take a "wait-and-see" stance for the rest.
Although world wheat supplies are now well balanced after shrinking last year, it wants to ensure that stubborn price rises in France are kept under control by playing safe with exports.

Exporters have been at odds with Brussels for more than two weeks over this policy, attacking its reluctance to grant more exports and watching local prices rise even further as farmers refuse to part with grain to exporters they know to be fretting.
"This is panic. The exporters are traumatised," one of them said, accusing the EU executive of "declaring war on the trade".

Traders are particularly bitter that the EU is now effectively selling wheat at a premium to U.S. soft red winter, a grade of wheat that is scarce this year and which the EU had previously publicised as a benchmark for its own weekly sales.
Thursday's subsidy award equated to an EU wheat export price of $151 per tonne on world markets, compared to soft red winter pegged at $147 or $148 per tonne depending on port premiums.
Some traders are looking for subsidies large enough to cover recent sales of $142 to $143 per tonne to North Africa.
One trader accused the European Commission of panicking in a week in which Washington reiterated recent threats to bring back back its own grain subsidies to fight European competition.

The European Commission says it is not its role to subsidise exports at any price and it must put internal price control first. It also has mounting budget pressures to pay for Europe's 11-month-old beef crisis.
EU officials have admitted, however, that the policy could lead to an increase in grain storage this year.

The EU, the world's third exporter behind the United States and Canada, is expected to export 15 to 16 million tonnes of wheat and flour products combined in the year to June 30. It has so far exported 11 to 12 million tonnes since last July 1.
-- Paule Bonjean, Tim Hepher, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5146
